title: Floppy infant with a fever and a rash
description: A mother brings her 9-month-old daughter, who is hot, floppy and has a new rash.

speaker.name: Busisiwe Zulu
speaker.style: Very worried and tired after a night without sleep.

patient.name: Lindiwe Zulu
patient.living_situation: Lives with her mother and two older brothers

presenting_complaint: Fever since last night, refusing feeds, floppy, and dark spots on the legs since this morning.
opening_line: Nurse, my baby is very hot and she is just lying there. And now there are these dark spots on her legs.
personality: Cooperative; she worries she waited too long.

history.onset: Fever started last night. This morning she was floppy and the spots appeared.
history.feeding: She refuses the breast since this morning and has had only a few sips.
history.urine_output: One small wet nappy since last night.
history.rash: Small dark red and purple spots on the legs and tummy that do not fade when pressed.
history.alertness: She is floppy, cries weakly and does not look at her mother.
history.weight: About 8 kilograms at her last clinic visit.

ground_truth.diagnosis: Septic shock with a non-blanching rash (probable meningococcal disease) in an infant
red_flags: poor feeding and few wet nappies
expected_actions: airway, high-flow oxygen, and intravenous or intraosseous access within 5 minutes
check the glucose; if below 3 mmol/L give 10 percent dextrose 2 millilitres per kilogram
give ceftriaxone 100 milligrams per kilogram (800 milligrams for 8 kilograms) intravenously, intraosseously or intramuscularly at once, within the first hour

give a balanced crystalloid bolus of 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram over 5 to 10 minutes and reassess after each bolus (crackles, enlarged liver), up to 40 to 60 millilitres per kilogram in the first hour where intensive care support is available
fluid-refractory shock: adrenaline infusion 0.05 to 0.3 micrograms per kilogram per minute
call for help and arrange urgent transfer to paediatric intensive care; infection-control precautions and notify the disease

vitals.result: Weight 8 kg. Capillary refill 5 seconds, cold mottled legs. Non-blanching purple spots on legs and abdomen. Weak cry.

aspirin.warning: Aspirin is not given to children for this problem; it risks Reye syndrome and bleeding.

iv_access.result: Access obtained (intraosseous in the left tibia after two failed cannula attempts); blood culture and bloods taken.

call_ambulance.result: Urgent transfer to paediatric intensive care requested. Estimated arrival 30 minutes.

escalate_doctor.result: Doctor informed using SBAR and coming now.

hints: Ask about feeding, wet nappies and the rash. Does it fade when pressed?
Look at her perfusion and check the glucose.
Access fast (consider intraosseous), antibiotics now, and a weight-based fluid bolus with reassessment.
Call for help early and plan transfer to intensive care.

ideal_approach: Recognise septic shock with a non-blanching rash: fever, floppiness, fast heart rate, poor perfusion and low pressure.
Airway, high-flow oxygen, intravenous or intraosseous access within 5 minutes; blood culture and glucose.
Treat glucose below 3 mmol/L with 10 percent dextrose 2 millilitres per kilogram.
Ceftriaxone 100 milligrams per kilogram at once.
Crystalloid bolus 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram, reassessing after each; adrenaline infusion if fluid-refractory.
Urgent paediatric intensive care transfer, infection control and notification.
debrief.model_answer: Lindiwe is 9 months old and 8 kg, with septic shock and a non-blanching purpuric rash, most likely meningococcal disease: fever 39.6, heart rate 192, blood pressure 62/34, capillary refill 5 seconds, floppy with a weak cry. Give high-flow oxygen, get intravenous or intraosseous access, take a blood culture and check the glucose (2.6 mmol/L: give 10 percent dextrose 16 millilitres). Give ceftriaxone 800 milligrams at once and a 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram (80 to 160 millilitres) crystalloid bolus, reassessing after each bolus. Call for help, arrange urgent transfer to paediatric intensive care, use infection-control precautions and notify the disease.
reflection_questions: What does a rash that does not fade on pressure tell you?
How did you calculate the bolus and the antibiotic dose?
Which signs would make you stop giving fluid boluses?
references: National Department of Health. Standard Treatment Guidelines and Essential Medicines List for South Africa: Paediatric Hospital Level. Latest edition.
Advanced Paediatric Life Support (APLS): The Practical Approach. Latest edition.
World Health Organization. Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children. 2nd edition.
debrief.review_note: Draft paediatric case written for the app. Doses and steps follow common paediatric emergency practice and need clinician review against the current South African guidelines before teaching use.

learning_objectives: Recognise septic shock in an infant
Give weight-based fluids, glucose and antibiotics
